title: Trace and Close
description: Trace a figure from a starting flag, find out whether it closes, and test whether a closed figure is a polygon by its straight sides.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

writeup.why: Trace a figure from a flag without lifting, find out whether it brings you back, and sort the closed figures with straight sides from the rest.
writeup.look: A sheet with one outline drawn on it, a flag and a tracing finger beside it, and a polygon gate with a ruler standing at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Trace and Close' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the figures traced against the figures this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each trace comes home or stops at a free end, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the fourth phase the two counters under the gate carry the sides and the corners, and this corner keeps the polygons counted. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The sheet fills the left of the working area, 640 by 430 at 64,214, on the panel colour, with one figure drawn on it as a deep blue outline at most 520 across. The flag stands in its tray under the sheet, 140 by 60 at 64,660, and is planted anywhere on the outline with one tap. The tracer, an amber fingertip, runs along the outline from the flag at walking pace and leaves an amber trail behind it; it never lifts and never jumps a gap. If it arrives back at the flag, the inside floods green from the middle outwards; if it meets a free end it stops there, that end glows vermilion as an end point, the trail stays drawn and nothing floods. The gap finder rests beside the flag tray, 140 by 60 at 216,660: a round glass 200 across that magnifies eight times whatever part of the outline it passes over, so a break a hair wide opens into a plain gap with an end point on each side. The name card lies beside it, 280 by 60 at 424,660, face down until a polygon has been counted, and then offers triangle for three sides and quadrilateral for four. The polygon gate stands at the right, 420 by 430 at 730,214, with its two questions written across its top in order, closed first and then straight sides only, and room for three figures in a row. A figure is taken in only if its trace came home; an open figure dragged to it is carried back to the sheet with its trail and its glowing end still drawn. Inside the gate a near-black straightedge is laid along each part of the outline in turn: along a straight part it lies flat and rings, and under a curved part a sliver of sky blue daylight shows and that part stays lit. Only a figure whose every part rang passes, and only then do the two counters under the gate open, sides at 730,660 and corners at 950,660, each 200 by 60: a side tapped lights amber and takes one on the side counter, and a corner tapped takes a vermilion dot, is named a vertex as the dot lands, and takes one on the corner counter. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a word pad wherever a figure is sorted, with keys reading open, closed, polygon, not a polygon, triangle and quadrilateral, and twelve number keys three across wherever a count of sides or vertices is asked for. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. A closed figure's outline meets itself exactly, with no gap anywhere, and an open figure's gap, once the gap finder has found it, is drawn wide enough to see at half size. Green appears inside a figure only after the tracer has brought it home, so the colour inside a figure is always the result of a trace and never a guess.
writeup.finish: The card shows the figures the child traced, the closed ones flooded with colour, and the polygons standing apart with their sides and corners counted.

phases.win: the tracer comes home to the flag and the inside floods with colour
phases.does: plants the flag on the outline and runs the tracer round without lifting
phases.goal: a closed figure brings a tracing finger back to where it started, and an open one does not
phases.says: Put the flag anywhere on the edge. Now trace it. Where do you finish?
phases.check: Away from the screen: draw a figure without lifting your pencil. Did you end where you began? Say whether it is open or closed.
phases.feels: the figure is closed when the trace comes home, not when it looks finished
phases.hands: Lay a skipping rope on the floor as a closed loop and chalk a mark on it. A child walks along the rope from the mark without stepping off, and the class says where they finish. Then lay the rope as a letter S and walk it again from one end.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: where did the tracer finish? Second rung, the phase's: is that the place where the flag stands? Third rung: the sheet is cut to one simple outline, a square or a hook, and the child traces it before the harder figure comes back. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: most closed figures met so far, a circle, a square, a heart, look finished at a glance, so the look stands in for the test.
wrong.move: decides a figure is closed because it looks round and whole, without tracing it.
wrong.screen: the flag is planted where the child left it and the tracer runs the outline at walking pace. This figure curls round without meeting itself, so the tracer stops at a free end, which glows, and nothing floods. The trail stays drawn from the flag to the free end, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside it, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a long, curling trace feels like going all the way round, and the place it finished is easy to lose sight of.
wrong.move: says an S is closed because the trace went a long way round before it stopped.
wrong.screen: the trail is replayed from the flag at the top end, and the flag and the free end at the bottom both glow, far apart, with a near-black bracket spanning the space between them. The tracer waits at the bottom end with nothing flooded, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a figure on the sheet with the flag waiting in its tray
phases.soWhat: A figure that starts and ends at the same place is closed, and one that starts at one place and ends at another is open.

phases.win: the gap finder opens the break wide, the free end glows, and nothing floods
phases.does: traces it, finds where the tracer stops, and passes the gap finder over that place
phases.goal: any gap, however small, makes a figure open
phases.says: It looked shut. Why did the tracer stop? Look closer there.
phases.check: Draw a circle with a tiny gap in it. Is it open or closed? Trace it with a partner to settle it.
phases.feels: however small the gap, the tracer cannot step across it
phases.hands: Lay the rope as a closed loop again, then pull one end back the width of a shoe. Ask whether the walker still gets home. Then draw a triangle on the board with one side stopping just short of a corner, too small to see from the back of the room, and let the class argue before a child traces it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where did the tracer stop? Second rung, the phase's: what is at that place when you look closer? Third rung: the gap is drawn wide first and then narrowed a step at a time, with the tracer run at each width. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a gap a hair wide makes no difference to how the figure looks, so it seems to make no difference to what the figure is.
wrong.move: calls a figure closed because its gap is too small to notice.
wrong.screen: the tracer runs from the flag and stops at the break, where the free end glows. The gap finder then passes over that place and opens the hairline into a plain gap with an end point on each side. The tracer waits at the gap with nothing flooded, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: finishing next to the flag looks exactly like finishing at it when the gap between them is a hair wide.
wrong.move: plants the flag at one side of the gap, traces round to the other side and calls that coming home, because the tracer ends up right beside where it began.
wrong.screen: the flag and the tracer's finishing place are both lit, and the gap finder passes over the space between them and opens it into a plain gap. The tracer is asked to step across and cannot: its trail stops at one end point, the flag stands at the other, and nothing floods. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

phases.screen: a figure that looks shut, with one break too small to see at first
phases.soWhat: Any gap, however small, makes a figure open.

phases.win: the ruler rings along every side of the polygon and leaves daylight under the curved part of the other
phases.does: sends each figure through the gate and watches the ruler test each of its parts
phases.goal: a polygon is a closed figure made of straight line segments only
phases.says: It is closed. Now are all its sides straight? Let the ruler check.
phases.check: Draw one closed figure that is a polygon and one closed figure that is not. What does the second one have?
phases.feels: the gate asks two questions in order, and a figure has to pass both
phases.hands: Cut out a triangle, a circle, a half circle and a triangle with a gap in one side. Hold a ruler against each part of each one and ask which have every part lying flat against it. Then ask which of those are closed, and say the whole rule aloud: a polygon is a closed figure made of straight line segments only.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: does the tracer come home on this figure? Second rung, the phase's: does the straightedge lie flat along every part? Third rung: the gate is cut to one figure at a time, and each question is lit in turn before the next figure comes. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: the definition the class has read speaks of figures made of straight segments and leaves out the word closed, and a gap at a corner is not a side, so nothing on the figure seems to break the rule.
wrong.move: calls an open triangle a polygon, because all three of its sides are straight.
wrong.screen: the open triangle is dragged to the gate and carried back to the sheet before the straightedge touches it, its trail still stopping at the free end, which glows. The gate's first question, closed, lights above its second, and the child's answer stays in the slot. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: one straight side is plainly there to see, and the curved part looks like one more side.
wrong.move: counts a half circle as a polygon because it has one straight side.
wrong.screen: the half circle passes the first question, its trace coming home and its inside flooding, and the straightedge is laid along each part in turn. It rings along the straight side and leaves a sliver of sky blue daylight under the curved part, which stays lit, and the figure is turned back from the gate with the child's answer still in the slot.

phases.screen: three closed figures waiting at the polygon gate, one of them with a curved part
phases.soWhat: A polygon is a closed figure made of straight line segments only, so a gap or a curved part rules it out.

phases.win: the two counters stop at the same number and the name card settles under the figure
phases.does: taps each side and each corner, then picks the name card
phases.goal: a polygon has as many corners as sides, and each corner, where two sides meet, is a vertex
phases.says: Count the sides. Now count the corners. What do you notice?
phases.check: Draw a polygon with six straight sides. Count its sides, then its corners. How many vertices does it have?
phases.feels: going round a polygon, sides and corners take turns, so neither count can get ahead of the other
phases.hands: Draw a closed figure with five straight sides on the board. A child walks a finger round it, saying side along each side and corner at each corner, while two others keep the two counts on their fingers. Tell the class that each corner, where two sides meet, is called a vertex, and ask why the two counts came out the same.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many sides have you tapped? Second rung, the phase's: where does each side meet the next? Third rung: the polygon is cut to a triangle, whose three sides and three corners are counted together before the larger polygon comes back. The number pad and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: a corner that opens wide hardly looks like a corner at all, so the eye slides past it along what seems one long side.
wrong.move: counts only the corners that look sharp and misses one where two sides meet at a wide angle.
wrong.screen: the straightedge is laid along each side in turn, and at the wide corner it cannot lie flat along both sides at once: it rings along one side, then turns to ring along the next. A vermilion dot drops at the turn as a vertex, the corner counter climbs to match the side counter, and the child's count stays in the slot beside them.

wrong.why: the page shows a square and a rectangle as its quadrilaterals, and the name sounds as if it belongs to them.
wrong.move: thinks only squares and rectangles are quadrilaterals, and calls a four-sided figure with no square corners something else.
wrong.screen: the four sides of the slanting figure are tapped and counted, and a vertex dot drops at each of its four corners, where two sides meet. The name card turns to quadrilateral, which counts sides and nothing else, and a square and a rectangle are set beside it under the same card. The child's name stays in the slot, nothing marked.

phases.screen: a polygon through the gate with its sides and corners not yet counted
phases.soWhat: A polygon has as many vertices as sides; a vertex is a corner, where two sides meet, and a four-sided polygon is a quadrilateral.

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the gap finder passes over the place where the tracer stopped. The glass swells the hairline break until it is a plain gap with a glowing end point on each side, the tracer's trail waiting at one of them and the flag at the other, and a thin tide of green that had started to creep in from the middle runs out through the gap and away. Pass the glass off and the break shrinks back to a hairline, but both end points keep glowing, so the figure stays open however shut it looks again. It can be done as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a figure lies on the sheet with its inside bare and the flag standing in its tray under the sheet. On the second a figure that looks shut lies on the sheet with the flag already planted on its outline, and the gap finder rests beside the flag tray, not yet passed over anything. On the third three closed figures, already traced home and flooded, wait in a row inside the polygon gate, one of them with a curved part, and the straightedge stands at the gate's edge. On the fourth a polygon stands inside the gate with its sides and corners unlit, the two counters under it at nothing and the name card face down. The running count at the top left holds the figures traced against the figures this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the flag, or the planted flag, or the first figure in the gate, or the polygon's first side, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where the tracer will finish. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any figure drawn freehand or with the ruler, with the tracer, the gap finder and the polygon gate open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on tracing figures home, the gap that makes a figure open, telling polygons from other closed figures, and counting sides and corners.
voiceLines: A figure on the sheet and a flag beside it. Where will the tracer finish?
Put the flag anywhere on the edge. Now trace it. Where do you finish?
It looked shut. Why did the tracer stop? Look closer there.
It is closed. Now are all its sides straight? Let the ruler check.
Count the sides. Now count the corners. What do you notice?
A new figure. Plant the flag before you decide anything.
Free play. Draw any figure, with the tracer, the gap finder and the gate open.
Put the flag back and trace again, slowly, without lifting.
Every figure traced home or stopped at its gap, and every polygon's sides and corners counted.

observations.why: A figure that ends where it starts has an inside with no way out, and the trace is what shows it.
observations.soWhat: A closed figure brings a tracing finger back to where it started, so trace it rather than judge it by eye.
observations.observe: The inside flooded only after the tracer came back to the flag.

observations.why: The tracer cannot jump, so any gap, however small, is a place where the figure ends.
observations.soWhat: Any gap makes a figure open, however small it is.
observations.observe: A break too thin to see stopped the tracer, and nothing flooded.

observations.why: The gate asks two things in order: closed first, then straight sides only.
observations.soWhat: A polygon is a closed figure made of straight line segments only, so a gap or a curve rules it out.
observations.observe: The gate turned an open triangle away before testing its sides, and turned away a closed figure with one curved part after testing them.

observations.why: Each side ends at a corner where it meets the next side, so going round, sides and corners take turns.
observations.soWhat: A polygon has as many vertices as sides, and a vertex is a corner, where two sides meet.
observations.observe: The side counter and the corner counter stopped at the same number on every polygon.

phases.screen: a figure on the sheet with the flag waiting in its tray
phases.win: the tracer comes home to the flag and the inside floods with colour
phases.traceback: The tracer runs from the flag, and the figure either floods or stops at a free end.
ladder: Did the tracer come back to the very point it left?
Where does the egg's line finish, next to where it began?
Follow the S with your eye. Does it ever meet its start?
Trace it again, slowly. Does the tracer reach the flag?
A closed outline has no free end anywhere on it.

phases.screen: a figure that looks shut, with one break too small to see at first
phases.win: the gap finder opens the break wide, the free end glows, and nothing floods
phases.traceback: The tracer stops at the break and the glass swells the hairline into a plain gap.
ladder: Look again at the corner the tracer never reached.
Send the tracer first. The glass belongs where the trail stops.
Take the loose end to the corner where the drawing began.
Look hard where the trail stops. What is sitting there?
A break only a hair wide still holds the tracer back.

phases.screen: three closed figures waiting at the polygon gate, one of them with a curved part
phases.win: the ruler rings along every side of the polygon and leaves daylight under the curved part of the other
phases.traceback: The straightedge is laid along each part in turn and the figure that passes stays in the gate.
ladder: Lay the straightedge along each part. Which one has no curve at all?
One of these never brings the tracer home, so the gate turns it away.
A curved part is not a straight line segment.
Did the tracer come home on the one you chose?
Does the straightedge lie flat along every single part?

phases.screen: a polygon through the gate with its sides and corners not yet counted
phases.win: the two counters stop at the same number and the name card settles under the figure
phases.traceback: Each side lights in turn and a vertex dot drops where two sides meet, until both tallies match.
ladder: Go round the figure once, and tap every side you pass.
A vertex is a corner. Tap each place where two sides meet.
One side runs from each dot to the dot next door.
Where does one side end and the next one begin?
Go round once, and stop where you set off.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The tracer runs from the flag, and the figure either floods or stops at a free end.
Phase 2: The tracer stops at the break and the glass swells the hairline into a plain gap.
Phase 3: The straightedge is laid along each part in turn and the figure that passes stays in the gate.
Phase 4: Each side lights in turn and a vertex dot drops where two sides meet, until both tallies match.

voice.opening: A figure on the sheet and a flag beside it. Where will the tracer finish?
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every figure traced home or stopped at its gap, and every polygon counted.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A leaf is drawn as one outline. A finger starts at its tip, goes all the way round without lifting, and comes back to the tip. Is the leaf open or closed?

question.en: Here is a leaf, drawn on the sheet as one outline. Choose your word before the tracer sets off.

items.planAnswer: Closed, because the tracing finger ends where it began

items.planQuestion: An egg shape is drawn starting and ending at the same point. Is it open or closed?

question.en: Now an egg shape is on the sheet. Choose again, and the tracer will settle it.

items.planAnswer: Closed, because it starts and ends at the same place

items.planQuestion: The capital letter S is traced from its top end without lifting. Where does the trace finish, and is S open or closed?

question.en: The capital letter S is on the sheet now. Pick a word for it.

items.planAnswer: At its bottom end, a different place, so S is an open figure

items.planQuestion: A figure has five straight sides, but at one corner the two sides do not quite meet. Is it closed?

question.en: A figure with five straight sides sits on the sheet, and the flag is already planted.

items.planAnswer: No. It is open, because the tracing finger reaches the gap and cannot get back to where it started

items.planQuestion: A circle is drawn with a small break in its curve. Is it open or closed?

question.en: Somewhere in this circle there is a break too thin to see. Put the glass on it.

items.planAnswer: Open, because the break stops the tracing finger getting back to the start

items.planQuestion: A rectangle is drawn, but its last side stops just short of the first corner. What must be done to make it closed?

question.en: This rectangle is drawn, but its last side stops short of the first corner.

items.planAnswer: Join the gap, so the last side meets the corner where the drawing began

items.planQuestion: Three closed figures are drawn: a circle, a figure with four straight sides, and a half circle. Which of them is a polygon?

question.en: Three closed figures wait on the sheet. Send the one the gate will let through.

items.planAnswer: Only the figure with four straight sides. The circle has no straight side, and the half circle has a curved side

items.planQuestion: Which of these is a polygon: a closed figure with five straight sides, an oval, or a triangle with a gap in one side?

question.en: Now three different figures. Send the polygon in.

items.planAnswer: Only the closed figure with five straight sides. The oval is curved, and the triangle with a gap is open

items.planQuestion: A closed figure has three straight sides and one curved side. Is it a polygon?

question.en: One closed figure is on the sheet. Look hard at every part of its edge.

items.planAnswer: No. A polygon is a closed figure made of straight line segments only, and this one has a curved side

items.planQuestion: A closed figure with four straight sides has its corners named D, E, F and G. What kind of polygon is it, and how many sides and vertices does it have?

question.en: A polygon lies on the sheet, its corners lettered. Tap round it, then give it its name.

items.planAnswer: A quadrilateral, with four sides and four vertices, D, E, F and G

items.planQuestion: A polygon has five straight sides, with its corners named L, M, N, O and P. How many vertices does it have?

question.en: The corners of this polygon carry letters too. How many vertices has it?

items.planAnswer: Five: L, M, N, O and P, one where each pair of neighbouring sides meets

items.planQuestion: A polygon has seven vertices. How many sides does it have?

question.en: Every vertex of this polygon is dotted already. Tap along its sides and count them.

items.planAnswer: Seven, because a polygon has as many sides as vertices

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.
